subsubtopic: PROPOSED FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity related to the unacceptable, frightening and shocking figures on unemployment released this date. Given the fact that, including the hidden jobless, this country now faces an actual unemployment rate of 11.5 per cent, or in other words over 1.3 million Canadians are out of work which in effect costs this country $17 million a day in lost GNP and $6 million a day in unemployment insurance, I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens):
That the Prime Minister immediately take steps to convene a first ministers' conference to deal with the critical problems of high unemployment and unsatisfactory real growth, hopefully to reverse the banana republic-like image this country presently enjoys.

speechtext:

In light of today's unemployment statistics showing unemployment levels having risen from last month's crisis levels and that employment in manufacturing has dropped 2.5 per cent in the past year yet government waste continues, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon):
That the government create jobs and lessen unemployment by introducing a new budget which should include income tax cuts for low and middle income earners to help stimulate demand for goods and services and in addition it should include a cut in federal sales taxes, particularly building supplies, to help stimulate demand for housing and thus create jobs in the construction and related industries.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the continuing serious problem of unemployment in all regions of Canada illustrated by a further rise in the seasonal unemployment figures, and given the fact that the June labour force statistics show a decrease in the labour force, in employment and in the participation rate, all of which reflect the growing problem of hidden unemployment with Canadians giving up looking for non-existent jobs, and in view of most economic forecasts indicating that the present level of unemployment will continue throughout 1977 and into 1978, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move a motion under the terms of Standing Order 43 concerning a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Figures from the Department of Manpower and Immigration released in June show that some 22 business firms have laid off
more than 6,000 workers due primarily to marketing problems-this was during June alone-and there are indications of further deterioration which will exacerbate the unemployment rate in industry to even more unacceptable figures than presently exist. That this House order the government to take immediate action to investigate problems causing these alarming lay-offs and to direct the expertise of the departments concerned with the object of rehabilitating the firms which are in difficulty and preventing further lay-offs.

speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. It is now an average of 50 per cent higher in the four provinces than in the rest of Canada. Even with the programs of the Department of Manpower, no serious turnaround of the present unemployment crisis has been achieved in Atlantic Canada. Can the Prime Minister indicate whether he has consulted with some of his key ministers with respect to the impact of their programs? Order. The House ought to be clear about two things. First, that the requirement, according to our precedents, for the tabling of a letter which has been cited or quoted is one which is directed against the ministry for the reason, obviously, that if a minister takes part in a debate in the House and is able to cite documents to his or her advantage, it is only in accordance with fair play and justice that those documents ought to be available to all the participants in the debate. That rule operates against ministers but not against other members.
In the second place, the right to table documents in this House is not one which can be used by members other than ministers of the Crown. I would be prepared to listen to argument that if an advantage has been gained by a member of the House, as a result of making reference to documents, the member concerned ought to be compelled to table those documents, whether he is a minister of the Crown or not, in order to equalize the advantage among all members participating in the debate and so that the discussion could continue on a fair footing. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege related to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had to say and what I regard as a petty, peevish and insulting reference to Premier Schreyer of Manitoba-I say that most seriously-as well as to myself as a member of the House.
During the question period, the Prime Minister said, on the one hand, that the Premier of Manitoba was betraying a confidence in revealing correspondence between himself and the Prime Minister, and that I, in turn, was compounding this by informing the House of some information which was of a confidential nature. I resent that, and I insist that the Prime Minister review the case and offer, in particular, the Premier
July 12, 1977

of Manitoba and myself an apology for the implication he has made and the inference to be drawn that we betrayed a confidence given by the Prime Minister.
In raising any question earlier in the House today I based it directly on a press statement which came out of the office of the Premier of Manitoba on Friday last. That press statement referred to a telex which was sent by the Premier of Manitoba in mid-May to the Prime Minister of Canada requesting a first ministers' conference to deal, among other things, with unemployment. More than a month later the Prime Minister replied that there would be no such conference held, at least immediately. In reply to that the Premier of Manitoba issued a public statement, and I assume, being a man of integrity, Mr. Schreyer, the Premier of Manitoba, was not revealing a confidential telex or telegram sent to him by the Prime Minister. Having made his own request public in the first place-and if the Prime Minister challenges this contention and I am mistaken, I will apologize to him-I am sure the Prime Minister replied to the premier not in a confidential way at all, but directly, in the normal course of correspondence. At any rate, in a press statement issued on Friday by the office of the Premier of Manitoba, the following paragraph appears:
The Prime Minister had replied June 22 that a first ministers' conference should be held some time in the coming months to deal with the issues raised by Premier Schreyer, but that such a meeting probably would require careful preparatory work in other ministerial areas. He-
That is a reference to the Prime Minister.
-also stated that job creation plans for the coming months were already close to completion when Mr. Schreyer's first telex of May 17 was received-
It seems to me very clear, Mr. Speaker, that if Premier Schreyer issued this statement publicly he was not betraying a confidence. Some very important questions have been raised, and I think the Prime Minister owes me an apology for suggesting that I am revealing something which is of a confidential nature. He also owes an apology to the Premier of Manitoba. Beyond that, on the very important issue of job creation, he owes an apology to the members of this House because the answers which he gave today did not make clear whether or not there were new job creation programs, as he suggested to Premier Schreyer there were.

speechtext:
1. The International Development Research Centre, a public corporation created by the Government of Canada in 1970 and financed through an annual Parliamentary grant, appropriated in December 1974 a sum of $644,000 to cover the preparation and start-up costs and the first three years of operation of the magazine, Famille et Developpement. It has been published quarterly in Dakar, Senegal, since January 1975. Actual expenditure to date is $486,900. The IDRC has so far been the sole contributor although it is likely that donor agencies in other countries may now be willing to join in providing additional support if it is required. Revenue from the sale of the magazine (paid circulation has reached almost 22,000, and readership is estimated at 200,000) is becoming a major factor in the financing of future operations and it is hoped that the publication will become self-financing in future.
2.	Famille et Developpement is the only mass-circulated, indigenous publication providing information on family health and development issues for the peoples of French-speaking Africa. The Editorial Committee as well as the editorial and production staff (except for the IDRC local administrator) is
[Mr. Goodale.J
entirely African. The publication provides information prepared and/or selected by Africans based on their perceptions of current African interests. The magazine does periodically have articles on the implementation of rural development programs in African and Asian countries; some of these articles refer to countries whose political and economic systems are different from those of the industrialized nations, including Canada, and reflect a concern with the existing economic disparities in the world. The magazine has never contained an attack on Canada or other industrialized nations. In one recent issue, the magazine contained a cartoon on the problems of aid tied to the economic or political interests of donor nations. The IDRC has protested the cartoon to the editorial staff of Famille et Developpement. Indications are that the publication has been extremely well received in Francophone African countries. Although the IDRC role in the publication is not direct and, therefore, not particularly visible, among those Africans who are aware of this Canadian support, the publication has brought considerable credit to the policies and programs of the Centre and thus to Canada's role in development aid.

Mr. Speaker, I am very concerned about the statement that has just been read in the House and it seems to me that now is the appropriate time to discuss it. Let me say in my introductory remarks that I assume these words were spoken by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in haste, or perhaps written by someone in his office, because knowing the minister as I do, 1 just cannot believe he could have been serious.
I want to bring to the attention of the House and record the fact that the bill was debated on second reading on May 11 and 12. Then it went to committee for eight days. We heard only two groups of witnesses in committee, one regarding the gun control section and one on invasion of privacy. All other witnesses were denied a hearing. The bill returned to the House for report stage and was debated on June 30, July 4, 11 and 12. On one of those days the debate lasted only about one hour and a half. Is the minister going to accuse this party, as he apparently has in his release, in full knowledge of the fact that the murder was committed in Ottawa? I feel deeply, as a Canadian, about this tragic occurrence, not only about what has happened in Ottawa but about the three incidents in Calgary in the last year and a half.
I bring to the minister's attention that one of the fundamental principles of administration of justice is that the Minister of Justice, in leading his department, must at all times show absolute integrity and honesty. In fact, those who have some knowledge of parliamentary history know that in the mother of parliaments the minister of justice is non-partisan because of the position he holds in administering justice.
Is the minister suggesting that the murder which took place last night-a tragic event for the young police officer who was killed, and for his family-as well as the incident in Toronto

and the one in Calgary to which I brought the attention of the House of Commons, were all caused because the bill which is now before the House was not passed? If that is what the minister implied, then we have reached a sorry state in the Department of Justice-and I must say, in frankness, that that is not the truth. The truth is that the murder which was committed in Ottawa involved the use of a long gun. As someone said in committee, there are six million long guns in Canada. Another member said there were 11 million. We know there are 2.5 million long gun owners who are not affected by this bill at all.
Therefore, to suggest that because we did not pass the bill yesterday-we debated the question of criminal law regulations and the matter of putting the onus on the Crown, not the accused-a murder was committed, is to place the blame on my friends in this party, something which I can only describe as shameful by the Minister of Justice and I hope he will apologize for it.

I would point out, with reference to the murders in Calgary, that the last one involved the use of a prohibited or restricted weapon. When the minister piloted the bill on capital punishment through the House he should have considered whether it might have been a deterrent. I leave that to him. He knows where I stood in this regard. On this side we had a free vote on capital punishment, but on the government side there was no free vote and every cabinet member lined up, to a man, to a woman. To suggest to us that we have caused crime to increase is shameful. Why will the government not set up an inquiry on crime in Canada, something for which we have asked over and over again?
Why will they not take a hard look at what kind of life a police officer must lead because of the crime rate in this country? Since this motion deals with peace officers and orders in council, we have pointed out that law that is drafted by orders in council, by cabinet or by an unknown and unnamed body, is improper. That is not the way to legislate criminal law. That was our message which rang through this chamber yesterday.
The second point which we argued yesterday was not one dealing with guns. It referred to the fact that in one of the provisions the government placed the onus on the accused. I pointed out that as in the "Cross" and "Wigmore" authorities on evidence, and for generations, our system of jurisprudence has been that a man or a woman cannot be found guilty in a criminal court unless the evidence shows they are guilty beyond a reasonable doubt-and the onus is always on the Crown. That was the argument we put forward yesterday. We put forward intelligent and intellectual arguments concerning liberty and freedom of Canadians. Then we were met with that kind of news release this morning. The only congratulation I can offer the Minister of Justice is that he did not include my name among those he mentioned. He knows I co-operated with him in the committee at every stage of the bill. To suggest that this bill would have stopped the murder in Ottawa yesterday,
July 12, 1977

or any other murder of a policeman, is utter nonsense and untruthful.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow on the same theme as that put forward by the two previous speakers who have pointed out that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has been derelict in his duty. Ele has been dishonest with the House of Commons and the country in suggesting that members on this side of the House were somehow connected with the most unfortunate murder last night. I would like to state in the House that there is a correlation in western countries between an increase in the rate of crime and murders and an increased rate of unemployment. If the Minister of Justice can say to us, as he did in his comments last night, that we are in some way guilty of the crime last night, then surely, because of the high rate of unemployment in the country at present, both the minister and the government have to accept the same kind of guilt because there is a relationship between crime and unemployment. However, I will not do that because I think we must maintain a higher level of integrity in the House, and to be blaming members for all the murders that are going on is certainly not the crux of the issue. But we must recognize that the minister made a most outrageous statement when he tried to blame members on this side of the House for the unfortunate deed last night.
I say that the amendment before us is one that is very important because it refers to the power to make changes by order in council. What the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) is saying in his motion could be said about many other bills, because the principle is extremely important. Last year over 3,300 orders in council were made by this government, none of which was referred to parliament. In the United Kingdom there were ten orders in council, all of which were referred to parliament. It is absolutely stupid to assume that we have control over our democratic process when in excess of 3,000 regulations can be made but never brought before parliament. We are not saying we oppose this legislation; we want an iron-clad guarantee about what the regulations will contain.
There are gun clubs in my constituency. 1 live in a farming and ranching constituency where guns are not used to kill people; they are used as tools to get skunks out from under chicken coops, or to kill coyotes coming into calving yards. We know, by the way this bill is being put forward, that right after we pass it the governor in council can change the length of time for which the registration period can exist, and the fees. The governor in council can make it prohibitive to obtain guns and can classify which guns are restricted and which are not restricted.
Every gun club I met did not mind having gun control. We ought to understand that. But we want to know if the gun control we have is one we can live with. Each day in this House there is an overbegging of the question. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tries to point out the differences
Criminal Code
between Canadians by saying that there are French and English, and English and French. He always focuses on the differences in an attempt to find some common cause in which we as a nation can join together so that we can forget our differences.
The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) has in his riding many constituents who are trappers by occupation-70 per cent in all. If the Prime Minister understood the development of the west and the use of guns in agriculture, he would recognize that this is a cultural question. The gun is a tool in many ways, but there are many tools which are used for killing people. People can be killed with knives, axes, saws, poisons, and in many other ways. If the government is sincerely interested in having a Criminal Code which would reduce the number of murders, it has to work with the psychology of people. It has to deal with child abuse. The governments of this country have been derelict in that respect. Much more needs to be done. We have definitions of child abuse which include broken bones and extreme bruising, but none of them touch the question of the psychological abuse of children. People have so psychologically degraded children that we find the mentality which causes the kinds of acts we read about in the newspapers today.
There is also a correlation between noise levels and tensions in people. There are some interesting articles dealing with urban development and noise levels. People who live in busy traffic areas and on the lower floors of apartment buildings have more tensions than others. Passing this bill and leaving all regulatory adjustments to orders in council gives no assurance to gun owners, and in fact may or may not have an effect on crime. While I do not subscribe to the conclusion of Judy LaMarsh that there ought to be one television station across the country, I think there is reason to believe that if our children are exposed to crime as entertainment, there will be problems. I think the government has an obligation to do something about that in the hope of preventing crime.
In Switzerland, all males over the age of 18 must own guns. There is in that country a very low crime rate when compared to the crime rates of the western nations. The toughest gun controls in North America are found in the state of New York. I need not comment on the crime rate there; we know it is very high.
Gun control in and of itself is not the answer. I spoke last year on Bill C-83. I detailed at great length many psychological, environmental and cultural changes which ought to be taking place in order to bring about the kind of human change which would give us different attitudes toward guns. We must remember that the gun is a cultural tool which is used in the occupation of many people in this country. If we are going to legislate gun control, the government should have the courage to make a definitive statement as to what the period of registration will be-and that should not be done by order in council. If that were done, our legislation would be far more effective. The legislation might be more effective if people were licensed for life.

July 12, 1977
Criminal Code
That could be done with people who own guns now, remembering that the same restrictive categories could still exist. Every new gun owner should take a course in which he could learn how to handle and properly care for a gun. From there we should work backwards. If a person gets a criminal record, he should lose his licence; if he becomes mentally ill, he should lose his licence; if he becomes addicted to drugs or alcohol, he should lose his licence; if he is careless with a gun and shoots a cow instead of a deer, for instance, he should lose his licence. In that way we could focus on that small section of society which handles guns dangerously.
The law being put forward by this government focuses on some 13 million gun owners and builds up a huge bureaucracy with power to make regulations, to increase fees at any time and in any amount, to shorten the period of registration, and to say to the farmer and the rancher that they may not have guns to get coyotes out of the calving yards. This legislation would allow the bureaucracy to tell northern Canada that the practice of hunting for a livelihood-a tradition which goes back to as far as the recorded history of the Indian and the Inuit- cannot be continued. I submit that that would be very unjust. The government cannot speak about culture in terms of language and forget all the other cultures which exist.
In conclusion, let me say that each and every one of us in this House wants to see the crime rate reduced. The motion we are debating does not say we must control all guns. It seeks to make sure that what we enshrine in legislation remains the law, that we are not voting on a certain provision today only to find it has been totally changed six months after the bill passes.
I have met with gun clubs of my constituency. One is in the city of Camrose, which hon. members may recall is the place of the great "hot dog festival." That gun club said it does not mind regulations so long as they do not infringe upon their right to collect guns, to shoot on a registered shooting range, to apply for a permit or to shoot on someone else's shooting range. They want to be allowed to use guns for sporting purposes. Similarly, ranchers in my constituency do not mind regulations so long as they are allowed to carry guns for the protection of their sheep and cattle and keep predators at bay. It is not as if they disapprove of Bill C-51; they do not trust the government. They are not against this legislation, per se, and I do not know how often I must repeat that. Apparently we must say it often for fear of being misinterpreted.
Let no one say the people of the western provinces are against this legislation per se. They will support such legislation if it is fair. They do not want to see enshrined in this bill some power giving a group of individuals power to change the law by order in council. They do not want bureaucrats alone to have power to put weapons into the prohibited class. Our people want to know the regulations, and if they are changed they want to know how they are changed. That a small group of people should have power to change these regulations arbitrarily is dreadful.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend yesterday taking part in the debate on this motion because it has to do with regulations. I spoke briefly on legislation by regulation. But the minister having earlier today issued a statement in which he included my name among others, I feel it my duty to speak.
July 12, 1977

I have been concerned over the years about the freedom of the individual and preserving our democratic way of life. I have seen the government opposite eroding, since 1968, our individual freedoms. Yesterday 1 spoke of government by regulation and said that regulations are never debated on the floor of the House of Commons. Some civil servant prepares them and a minister passes them. They are promulgated, as the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said, in the dark of the night. Mr. Speaker, parliament is the place to debate legislation. Parliament tells the people of this country what laws are in process of enactment. But when you make law by regulation, not only do the people of Canada not know the law but many legislators, many members of parliament, do not know it. How can the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) say that because members of the opposition debated this bill they are somehow responsible for yesterday's tragic death of a policeman?
I gather, from reading the statement he made over the air, that the minister is suggesting members of the opposition have no business to debate a bill. The reason I and other members of parliament are here is to debate bills, examine legislation, make amendments and let the people of Canada know what is the law. That is democracy, the right to speak your mind, to say what you think. However, the Minister of Justice, the man who should be concerned about our democratic way of life, is suggesting that members of the opposition should not be speaking in a debate in this House.
I wonder what Canada is coming to, when a responsible minister of the Crown suggests that parliamentarians, opposition members, should not be speaking on a bill. 1 give the minister notice that as long as I am here in Ottawa as a member of parliament, I intend to debate every bill and every amendment that I believe is important to my constituents and the people of Canada. There is no way the minister or any other member on that side will prevent me from debating legislation.

In his statement the minister made reference to the fact that yesterday we were discussing the safe storage of guns. He said we were weakening the provision relating to the safe storage of weapons. If the minister would care to take the time to read the minutes of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, he would see that I made specific inquiries of him and addressed very genuine concerns to him on the subject of safe storage of guns. I feel qualified to address myself to that subject because I have much greater knowledge of that subject than the minister and half of his people. However, the minister would seek to distort and twist the truth. We went on to say we were concerned about reducing the sentences for the use of guns. He said that without the benefit of any explanation. It was a flat statement, with nothing attached to it. The minister knows that in debate yesterday this House was concerned with only one point of one amendment when dealing with the subject of reduced sentences. That was that the sentence for a person having a prohibited weapon should be greater than the sentence for a person in violation of the law with a restricted weapon. One weapon you clearly cannot have. One weapon is prohibited. The other is restricted. That was the only reference.
When it comes to reducing sentences for the use of guns, I draw Your Honour's attention to statements I made previously in this House at an earlier stage when we were dealing with this bill. I recounted, for the benefit of the minister and hon. members, that at my personal urging two of my constituents preferred charges against a big game outfitter in northern British Columbia who threatened them with an unregistered revolver. I put this on record and I challenge the minister to explain why it would happen. My constituents appeared in court in Fort Nelson, not once but three times, at a cost to the taxpayers of goodness knows how many dollars. There were three separate hearings before the judge. When they finally appeared on the issue of an unregistered gun, having a gun in a place other than a dwelling place, after a severe reprimand from the judge the accused was relieved of any further burden of responsibility. There was no fine, no jail sentence. What possible use can there be to legislation in which we seek out

July 12, 1977
Criminal Code
the criminal, if the courts are not going to impose a sentence that has any meaning?
1 have asked the minister to provide this House with statistics as to how many people were accused of contravening the firearms legislation, how many were sentenced in the last year, and what was the manner of the sentence. For example, was it a token fine, or a jail sentence. I have been met with stony silence from the minister. I am certain that if the facts were disclosed to the public we would find that the courts are not carrying out the mandate they have been given. That is the concern of Canadians. It is not the legislation; it is the interpretation of the law and the manner in which it is carried out.
The minister's conduct last night can only be described as ghoulish, callous and macabre. No one in this House regrets more than I do the events that occurred in this city last night. I share, with my fellow members, respect for the law and for the police who carry out the law, sometimes in very dangerous and difficult circumstances. I share that respect and I share that concern. I shared it enough to vote in favour of capital punishment, which the cabinet opposed. But it cannot go unsaid that the minister, throughout this afternoon's expressions of concern by those members he affronted, has failed to address himself to that issue and to make apologies for his statement.
I have said enough on this subject. I am sure the people of Kootenay West will understand my outspoken reaction. I hope the minister will withdraw his comments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking on this bill may be a pure waste of time. It is obvious to me that those who drafted it have not done their homework. If they had, there would not be clauses in it to say that the most important part would be implemented by regulation. Before going on to that, I want to echo the remarks made by some of the previous speakers. They were all from one party. I do not belong to that party, nor to any party in this House. But for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to have the audacity last night to make the remarks about members of this House in such a terrible way is certainly unethical and improper.
Parliament is the place where we debate and discuss legislation and where we should be able to discuss regulations. We try to protect the rights of individuals. I am sure every member of parliament sympathizes with the family of the deceased policeman from Ottawa. Also we, as members of parliament, represent our constituents and purport to live as a democratic state. And this place is purported to be a place where we protect that democratic state by the right of debate and the right of free speech. I suggest that the very man who should be most interested in the protection of individuals and their rights, violated one of the most important rights, the right to speak in parliament, last night and this morning by doing just what he did. I and other members of parliament are supposed to express the views of our constituents, and we should express

them sincerely, frankly and honestly. I repeat, the remarks of the minister were deplorable; they were unethical.
But orders in council-what are they? They take us back to the days of King John and the Magna Carta. The whole purpose of the Magna Carta was to get rid of orders in council or arbitrary decrees of government. These orders in council permit the delegation of power to the cabinet, in effect to the bureaucracy, to operate and provide criminal law in this country. How much can we belittle parliament? How much can we belittle the sense of our constituents? I recall that 31 months ago, in December, 1974, two policemen were killed in my constituency. I did not hear anyone in this House say then that the death of those two policemen resulted from anything that any member of parliament did here or did not do. They were brutally killed. They were killed by vehement criminals. This bill would not have saved their lives. This bill would not have saved the life of that policeman last night, either.
For the Minister of Justice to leave the impression with Canadians generally and, in particular, with people in the Ottawa area, that anyone who opposes this bill or is not prepared to support it is responsible for the acts of criminals who commit murder, is just not proper; it is unethical. For the Minister of Justice, who holds the highest office of any barrister or lawyer in this country, to make a statement of that kind and to involve members of parliament in statements of that nature, is most improper.
Before coming here I acted as defence counsel. I still practise law, and I am not ashamed of it. I also acted as criminal prosecutor. I had some respect for those who achieved the office of minister of justice, whether under provincial or federal jurisdiction, but after hearing those remarks last night and hearing them again this morning, I have my doubts. It is the type of thing which reduces respect for law and order in our country, to hear a minister of justice make a statement such as the minister made. It should be withdrawn very apologetically.
A good number of my constituents not only oppose the legislation by order in council with respect to this bill, but with respect to any bill. One hon. member drew attention to the fact that in 1976 more than 3,200 orders in council were passed in Canada at the federal level. Only ten went through in Great Britain. This is no way to operate criminal law. The problem with the bill is that it is a catch-all bill; it has everything in it, and not much of any of it is good. I repeat, the Minister of Justice, in presenting this bill, has delegated so much of its powers to order in council that it is, to me, a clear indication that the government is not ready, has not done its homework and is not prepared to tell us what is in the substantive part of the bill.
Gun control is really not the answer to the problems of law and order and crime in this country. My feeling is that the legislation is likely to create more problems, more bureaucracy and more difficulty than we have now. We are taking a backward step, first by introducing gun control; second, by legislating by regulation or order in council. I would suggest that the amendment is quite a proper one, although I am not
July 12, 1977

sure I would even support the amendment if it meant the bill would go through.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on motions Nos. 15 and 16. Motion No. 16 relates to section 103( 1 )(d), which reads as follows:
-mail a copy of the record and inventory relating to restricted weapons to the commissioner or to any person authorized by subsection 106.2(5) to issue a permit to carry on the business in accordance with any request in writing made by the commissioner or any such person.
They are being asked to keep inventories of the number of firearms they have, and to keep a record of transactions which take place. This record and inventory must be produced for inspection at the request of any police officer, police constable or other person authorized by regulation. In addition, it is being recommended that subparagraph (d) be removed. Prohibited weapons would include all hand guns with the exception of some air pistols. This has been a matter of record for some time. As far as registered guns are concerned, the system has been to make a registration, and the registration carries the documentation for the gun which is kept by the person. There is also a record kept by the store, the agent, the gunsmith or whoever may be running the business. This would also involve a collector. He is required to keep in a safe place a record of those guns. If a police officer asks for that record, it will contain such things as the time, the day, the name, the address, the type of weapon and the serial number of the weapon.
This matter was left with the gun shop or the gun agent, and it seems to me it was a fairly satisfactory way of operating as there is seldom any need for this information unless a question arises concerning stolen guns or guns used for an illegal purpose. If we made them restricted weapons, some collectors and museums would still be able to have them, as provided for in other parts of the bill. We would need a larger bureaucracy to deal with the information sent in from gun shops, which would probably be fed into a computer and made available to all police agencies in this country and to Interpol. This clause indicates that a business is not only one that deals in restricted weapons, but also one that is involved in the manufacturing, buying or selling wholesale or retail, or in importing ammunition. The clause requires that records shall be kept of transactions with respect to such weapons or firearms in a form prescribed by the commissioner, and then goes on to indicate that ammunition is included.
In northern Ontario we have a large tourist industry, and it has been one of the perks of good Conservatives who run grocery stores or an outfitters operations to sell licences for hunting partridge, deer and moose. Usually they sell the licences and the ammunition, small shotgun shells for duck
Criminal Code
hunting, and two or three kinds of shells for bear hunting, as well as .22 ammunition. It is a fairly lucrative business. The goods are easy to store, but if they have to keep records and report periodically, there will not be much advantage.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: You are misreading the bill.

Maybe, but it seems to me that if they have to send in records relative to restricted weapons, they will probably have to do it for other weapons and ammunition as well. None of these small stores has facilities for safe keeping, but I do not think anybody goes in to steal ammunition. I only know of a few instances of theft of ammunition. Usually there is a break-in for another reason, and ammunition is just picked up.
I am concerned when guns are not kept in a safe place in stores. For that reason I am very happy about the regulations which mean Canadian Tire, Eaton's, Simpson's and such stores will no longer display guns on the counter like a bargain in shirts or sweaters. That is just asking for trouble. It is surprising the number of guns that are stolen at Canadian Tire stores-sometimes by the staff, but mostly because somebody just picks them up. I think if you went into a hardware store and asked for centre-fired .38 shells, you would get some pretty strange looks, because they are obviously for a revolver and there is small call for such ammunition as most collectors and gun clubs do their own loading. What we are really talking about is limitation of shotgun shells and hunting rifle shells.
If all this reporting is required, it will put some people out of business. Maybe that is a good idea. I think there is merit in hardware stores selling guns, because they are equipped to do it and have staff who know something about guns. Some time ago I bought a 303 sporting rifle for $25 at Simpson's in Toronto. That can be a pretty powerful gun, depending on the type of ammunition used with it. They had hundreds of them, and anybody could walk out with an armful because, of course, they cannot be wrapped. Maybe we should limit their sale and the sale of ammunition. But we should not limit it to the point that everyone has to report every time they sell a box of shells, shotgun shells or 12, 16 or 20-gauge shot for birds. That should not be restricted. The minister may not even intend to restrict it, but he has left it up to the commissioner and the commissioner will damn well want to do that. He will want to have the whole thing under his jurisdiction, because it will mean more work, more employees and, therefore, a higher grade in the civil service.
I am being realistic. I know that if you get more work, you have more people under you. Hasn't every member of parliament found that out? It seems to me that is what the commissioner will do. So I support the withdrawal of the provision requiring the reporting of ammunition. I would like to hear the minister indicate what he thinks of the system we now use for registering prohibited guns, fully automatic rifles, Thompson sub-machine guns, Bren machine-guns, in operating condition. The gunsmith enters each transaction involving such guns in

July 12, 1977
Criminal Code
his books. He records the time and place of the sale, and he has the signatures. The inspector is allowed to look at the book at any time.
My colleague and I were in a gun shop the other day. I asked the gunsmith how many guns he had sold and he told me that he never counted them. But he showed me the book and asked me how far I wanted to go back, two or three years. If an inspector wanted to see when a certain transaction took place, he would see the time a gun was bought or sold recorded in the book and the serial number of the gun. The information is all down there. If that information were to be sent to the commissioner, he would establish a key punch operator and other people necessary to put the information into a computer. One day we will have computer tapes coming out of our ears. Instead of getting a report, we will get computer tapes.
I honestly believe that we will have problems in registering ammunition. There is no question that ammunition is dangerous, but I have not heard of anybody except very small kids taking gunpowder out of ammunition and making a bomb out of it. 1 have not heard of other people doing that. Ammunition is only involved in the use of guns. We are establishing control over gun transactions; therefore I do not think we need to control ammunition. If we get to the point where all transactions are made through the commissioner and are registered periodically, we will be heading toward the proposition which I believe is at the back of the minister's mind, that all guns be confiscated and eliminated. Surely that is not what this bill intends, and it is not what I wish accomplished. So I hope the minister can indicate that he does not wish to have all these transactions recorded. I would like him to tell us whether the system used for prohibited weapons has been adequate.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments in connection with motion No. 17. Basically, it would delete the word "advertise" in subsection 6(a) as well as the word "ammunition". Proposed section 103(1) concerns people involved in the manufacturing, buying or selling at wholesale or retail, etc., of restricted weapons, and subsection (2) speaks of lost, mislaid or stolen weapons. Frankly, I do not think it is possible to control every sale or transaction

involving ammunition, because ammunition is bootlegged in hunting caps, and so on. Therefore, we are kidding ourselves if we think we can enforce every such regulation the governor in council will make.

Motion No. 18.
That Bill C-51, An Act to amend the Criminal Code, the Customs Tariff, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act and the Prisons and Reformatories Act, be amended in Clause 3 by striking out line 24 at page 27 and substituting the following therefor:

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to amend the bill in order to require a person receiving an application for firearms acquisition certificate to make a decision within a reasonable period of time. My amendment asks that the official make that decision within 15 days.
The firearms acquisition certificate is the keystone of this bill. It is required by those wishing to purchase certain types of firearms, a much enlarged category as a result of the government's proposal in this regard, and will affect many hundreds of thousands of citizens. It will result in the establishment of a much larger bureaucracy.
We know how the bureaucrats work, if I can use that term. In many cases it is questionable whether they do work. In any event a great number of people are experiencing an ever-increasing amount of delay in having their requests dealt with by governments at all levels.
As long as we have governments like the present one which wants to encroach further and further into the lives and activities of decent, law-abiding citizens, we will have more and more bureaucrats dealing with the reasonable requests of these people. The bureaucrats will say that they are overburdened because there are too many applications to be dealt with. They will make all sorts of excuses for delaying legitimate requests.
Something should be written into this law to require these officials to exercise their duties within a reasonable period of time. When an application for a firearms acquisition certificate is made, it should be dealt with within 15 days. I am open to suggestions of a reasonable nature as to whether that time limit is appropriate. I feel it is. If you require a firearm, you want it before the hunting season is over so that you can enjoy the benefits of that part of the country in which you live. Otherwise, you will have to wait until the next season.
One criticism of this bill is that it is very restrictive for the large majority of Canadians who wish to enjoy the benefits of

July 12, 1977
Criminal Code
this country. That is one of the great advantages of Canada, that it is spacious. There are large recreational facilities for hunting and the like. However, it will be much more heavily regulated by the federal government as a result of its reaction to very emotional concerns.
We are dealing with this as a matter of emotion rather than looking at the practicalities. As much practicality as possible should be built into this legislation. I know that it would be very difficult because this legislation is impractical from beginning to end. Nevertheless, wherever we can, we should try to do this. I suggest a time limit on these people so that the ordinary citizen can exercise his legal right and force them to act within a reasonable time. subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in support of this amendment which deals with a most important aspect of the bill, presuming that the legislation will aid in the prevention of homicides. Most of this prevention would be as a result of control officers being aware of an applicant fo- a gun certificate who may be unstable, have a criminal record or some such thing. I suspect that a criminal would not apply for a certificate. He would obtain a gun in the same way he has always done.
There may be an occasional applicant who is mentally unbalanced. Speaking from my experience, if I had to decide as to whether such a person should have a gun certificate, I do not know if 1 could make a very good guess. Many people might be suspected of being unstable, but they get along pretty well in society, staying out of trouble.
If the legislation is to have any value at all, the government will have to depend on the actions and judgment of those who are issuing these certificates. But there is nothing here to specify the time available in which they can make up their minds when a person who applies for a certificate will get one. Suppose these officials are uncertain whether to issue a certificate or not. Will they spin out time by making up some bureaucratic excuse, allowing the applicant to wait indefinitely? There should certainly be some means whereby the officials, or the minister, will be required to make up their minds within a certain period whether a person should receive a certificate or not.
It may be that a period of two weeks is not sufficient. If the case has to be investigated, it might take some time for information to be gathered from outlying areas. Nevertheless, a time limit of some sort ought to be set. My hon. friend from Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) has told us that he is easy about the precise extent of that time limit. The minister might consider some other period. I suspect that in most instances of bureaucratic delay applicants are kept waiting because a decision is not altogether easy to make, because it might turn out badly, because it is in a dicey area and events might reflect on the judgment of those concerned. Nevertheless, somebody has to make decisions, and all this amendment says is that within a

reasonable period of time the official must give an applicant a yes or no answer and that, if he does not, the citizen concerned should have recourse to the law to demand that such an answer be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an issue which was examined very thoroughly in the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. There are really two sides to it-whether there should be a legislated minimum period before which no certificate can be issued, or whether there should be a legislated maximum period within which a certificate must be issued, or at any rate within which the application must be decided.
After careful consideration, both points of view were rejected by the committee and the bill was left as it is. The hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne), who has been active in committee, and in whose riding there have been four impulse murders in the recent past, pushed very hard for a minimum period. Other members pushed for a maximum period. I think things are best left as they are. The design of the scheme is such that the requirements of the scheme act as an effective cooling off period as a means of helping to prevent impulse murders; people would not be able to buy a gun on impulse with the intention of using it against themselves or others. The administrative procedures would be worked out by the chief provincial firearms officers to be responsive to the public need.
In cases where the application form itself or the computer check shows no information which is adverse to the applicant,
I am content that a certificate can be issued quickly. But if there is some adverse material in the criminal record to check, or if the applicant has undergone mental treatment in connection with symptoms of violence, it might not be possible to issue a certificate within a 15-day period; there might be a number of factors which the licensing officer would wish to consider and a good deal of information which he might want in his possession before making a decision. If a statute of limitation were placed upon the period I am sure that, in administrative terms, the result would be that if there were any adverse information whatsoever affecting an application, rather than take a risk the licensing officer would simply say no within the required period, though if examined thoroughly the material available would enable the officer, given time, to grant the certificate. I think that would create a hardship for people who might, upon close examination of their applications, be entitled to own a firearm.

He will have to make his application to one of the RCMP officers in the area, probably the only officer there, who has more work than he can handle. speechtext:
Motion No. 20.
That Bill C-51, an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Customs Tariff, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act and the Prisons and Reformatories Act, be amended in Clause 3 by striking out line 33 at page 31 and substituting the following therefor:
"(i) to protect life or property,".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise objection to the way this provision is drawn by the minister and suggest to him that by adding the word "property" he will have a better bill. It seems logical that when these permits are issued they are to be issued to people in order that they may be in possession of a firearm in the event of attacks by humans, or in the odd case by animals such as bears and so on.
However the minister has not made a provision for property. For example, a farmer who has a field of grain would not be issued with a licence in order to protect his crop from being eaten by deer. Even though it would be permissible under the provincial games act to protect his property by chasing them off in some way, he would not be able to get a gun because his life is not at stake. The minister seems to have the idea that he will protect him, but that man could starve to death during the winter. Many questions can be raised about this narrow definition of protecting life.
There will be very few permits issued. The farmer's property is his means of income and livelihood. If there is a threat to it, such as some person threatening to burn his place down, under this act he would not be able to obtain a firearm for protection.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]

Mr. Speaker, the amendment proposed by the bill is quite simple. I recognize that the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) is endeavouring to be constructive but, with respect, I think he misunderstands it.
Formely under the Criminal Code a person could be issued a carrying permit for sidearms for the protection of life or property. Under the proposed bill a permit would only be issued to carry or wear sidearms for the protection of life. Police authorities across the country have said, and we believe, that protection of property with firearms is not a desirable thing. People trying to protect themselves and their property with sidearms are usually more of a menace to themselves than to an intruder. We have all read over and over again the advice that the police give, that if someone breaks into your house the best thing you can do is keep perfectly quiet.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE

Mr. Speaker, the response given by the minister would lead one to believe that the intention is eventually to get rid of all restricted weapons. He talks about carrying a side-arm. This section does more than refer to carrying sidearms; it refers to a person being able to have a sidearm in his possession. I have a pistol in my possession and I have a permit, a registration certificate. If I had to establish that the reason
Criminal Code
that I have that weapon in my possession is to protect my life,
I would probably have to turn it in to the police. If the minister is saying that this only refers to people carrying sidearms, then it refers to restricted weapons, which is more than revolvers because it covers automatic weapons as well. I do not think the minister has read the bill.
A restricted weapon, according to the definition in the bill
is:
a)	Any firearm, not being a prohibited weapon, designed, altered or intended to be aimed and fired by the action of one hand,
b)	Any firearm that
(i)	is not a prohibited weapon, has a barrel that is less than eighteen and one half inches in length and is capable of discharging centre-fire ammunition in a semi-automatic manner, or
(ii)	is designed or adapted to be fired when reduced to a length of less than twenty-six inches by folding, telescoping or otherwise, or
c)	Any firearm that is designed, altered or intended to fire bullets in rapid succession during one pressure of the trigger and that, on the day which this paragraph comes into force, was registered as a restricted weapon and forms part of a gun collection in Canada of a bona fide gun collector,
I question whether the minister has read the bill and understands what it is all about. We have had regulations and laws respecting restricted weapons for many years. There have been no real problems with respect to restricted weapons. What we ask for here is simply to leave the principle as it exists at present to allow a person to obtain a registration certificate if it is required to protect his life or, as the old code says, "or property".
It seems to me that what is attempted here is a gradual restriction of the ownership and use of firearms. I can see the minister looking at me through the curtains. He seems to be moving in and out as he feels like it. When things get hot, he moves out. I suggest there has been no problem at all with restricted weapons. The minister wants to make some problems with respect to the legislation. What I am saying is that the provisions as they stand right now are adequate. They will not prevent crimes from being committed. If a criminal wants to get a gun, he can get one, and no amount of gun legislation or restriction will prevent him from getting one.

If you have a loaded hand gun in your night table drawer, you are very likely to shoot a member of the family. gun in the till in his small corner grocery store. There are too many small grocers who have guns in their tills. No, but I would not want to use a hand gun on a grizzly bear either. I would want to have something better than that, or I would be making tracks faster than the bear.
The minister has not justified the argument that we should not protect our property with sidearms, and I am one of those who do not believe we should be carrying hand guns to protect our property. However, I suggest that it is not in the interests of a modern urban society to have the right to carry guns for the purpose of protecting our lives or our property. If we agree with that, we must also agree that we should not be able to hire people to do what we cannot do ourselves.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest and some amusement to some of the remarks made by the minister and by some other hon. members tonight. On the advice and recommendation of members of the local police department in my constituency I had occasion to carry firearms for a considerable length of time and to be trained in their use. This is so with my wife and daughter as well. Criminal Code
particularly where there have been incidents which indicate the requirement to protect life and property.
It seems to me that our lives and our property are part and parcel of our possessions in this world and, by golly, by doing this we are taking away a great deal from people who are licensed and who have certified firearms. You do not have the right to shoot trespassers in this country, and all of the people who think that by having a gun they are protecting themselves should know that the statistics overwhelmingly show that that simply escalates the rate of violence and encourages the criminal element to go to houses with guns. ENERGY-OIL-SUGGESTION EXTRA REVENUE BE PLACED IN FUND TO BE USED ONLY FOR EXPLORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 27 in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) I directed the following question to the government House leader, who was then Acting Prime Minister:
Is it correct that the increase in oil and gas prices recently announced by the federal government will result in windfall revenues of some $1 billion going to oil companies, largely foreign owned, without any obligation on their part to use any of this money for exploration for and development of oil and gas resources?
I will not read the rest of the question. It is in Hansard. The reply of the acting Prime Minister was only that he was not in a position to confirm the alleged facts pointed out by me. He said that my question was in the nature of a representation which would be considered.
In announcing a couple of weeks ago an increase in the Canadian crude oil price of $1 a barrel as of July 1 and three subsequent $1 per barrel increases at six-month intervals, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that the purpose of these subtantial increases was to encourage development and production of oil resources. But how would these objectives be achieved if, of the added revenues as a result of these increases, 24.6 per cent-that is, in effect, 25 per cent- would go to the oil companies, 48.4 per cent to the oil provinces, and 27 per cent to the federal government, and if in fact the oil companies would get their 25 per cent without doing anything extra at all by way of exploration and development? How would this windfall to the oil companies create increased exploration and production activity?
Well, Mr. Speaker, in today's Globe and Mail a letter appeared signed by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, which constitutes an attempt to give the kind of information I was seeking in my question. First of all, his letter confirmed the provision of the additional revenues I have just mentioned. However, it disputes the claim that the 25 per cent to the oil companies would total $1 billion over the next 12 months. The letter claims, instead, that this is a gross amount and the net amount after royalties to the producing provinces would be only about half of this. Additional amounts from these revenues would go as federal taxes, the exact sum depending on the extent to which the industry re-invests the additional cash flow. But, Mr. Speaker, from the letter it seems clear that after taking taxes and royalties into account, the oil industry would still be left with as much as several hundred million dollars at the very least without doing any exploration and development in addition to what they are doing now, or would be doing anyway.
July 12, 1977

If the purpose of the increase is to bring about increased production of our petroleum resources, why should the oil companies get any additional revenue, even one dollar, that is not used for exploration and development, to bring about such increased production?
The oil companies, Mr. Speaker, have increased their profitability substantially in recent months. The figures indicate a better profit performance than our secondary manufacturing industry. If the purpose of the increase in oil prices is to encourage conservation by consumers and industry, the second reason for the increase presented by the minister when he announced it, surely there is no sound reason why the oil companies should benefit from this objective. Surely if this is the purpose, additional revenues from the price increase should be used by the government for further research into alternative energy sources, particularly renewable ones, and into better methods of conservation. They should be used to assist low income Canadians to insulate their homes, to provide meaningful financial assistance for them to do this to a greater extent than that made possible by the forthcoming federal government home insulation program, rather than letting this money go into the coffers of the oil industry.
The minister in his letter in today's Globe and Mail said his cash flow monitoring bill presently before parliament will give him the information necessary to evaluate oil industry behaviour. But if after this legislation is passed it is found the industry did not use the additional income from these oil price increases for exploration and development, there is no provision in the bill that I am aware of for getting this money back. It is gone forever. And even though the minister argues the information provided as a result of his bill will prepare the government to take corrective measures, and these are his exact words in the letter, there is no commitment from the government as yet to take such measures, or any indication as to what they might be.
Finally, in his letter the minister argues that the oil price increases will prevent our secondary industry from expanding, and I quote him, "into activities where competitive advantage depends on artificially depressed prices." Mr. Speaker, this is turning reality upside down. If through proper government policy oil prices reflect the actual costs of production and exploring for our own Canadian energy resources, plus a reasonable return, surely these prices will not be artificially depressed. The really artificial prices are those set by the OPEC oil cartel, prices which have no relationship to the cost of production and reasonable returns.
Canadian consumers and workers would, I am sure, prefer that the minister and the government were not seemingly so willing to bring our prices up to the level of the articificially high prices set by the OPEC cartel.

And if the industry continues investing in 1977-78 at the same rates as in 1976, the added revenues of nearly half a billion, after deduction of the operation costs and royalties, will go into capital investments in Canada. The government is taking all necessary steps to protect the interests of the Canadian consumer and has instituted a petroleum industry monitoring program. In order to follow more closely the reinvestment behaviour of the petroleum industry, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has introduced the Petroleum Corporations Monitoring Act, Bill S-4, which provides legislative authority for the collection of cash-flow and re-investment data from members of the Canadian petroleum industry. This program has indicated an increase in reinvestment from 66.9 per cent in 1973 to 76.4 per cent in 1976 for a select sample of 35 leading members of the petroleum industry.
In the absence of any alarming divergence from this encouraging trend, the government will continue to support the view that the corporate sector is the best judge of the risks involved and the best judge of what and where to invest. The above-mentioned monitoring bill will also provide the minister with the information necessary to propose changes to the present system should future investment behaviour of the industry prove to be in contrast with our national interest.

I made a trip to Dorval today to visit the Air Canada overhaul and maintenance base there and to meet with the Canadian Aviation Fellowship, an organization which has provided me with information with regard to the 2,600 employees who are requesting a transfer from the province of Quebec.
The Canadian Aviation Fellowship was formed about six months ago by a group of Air Canada employees who were very concerned about radical political events occurring in Quebec which would have a profound effect upon their future. Since its beginning the CAF has expanded considerably and is an official federally chartered organization with approximately 1,000 card carrying members located mainly in Quebec. Their membership consists of people in all areas; mechanics, pilots, flight attendants, ramp workers, clerical, and management. In addition to their card carrying members, they have the full support of several thousand other aviation workers throughout the Canadian aviation industry, many of whom have not formally joined the CAF out of fear of reprisals.
There seems to be some support for their request to move out of the province of Quebec. The federal government and Air Canada are presently completing a SI5 million hangar in Winnipeg, and Air Canada has recently been moving maintenance personnel to Toronto. I have here a copy of a letter dated December 1, 1976. It is signed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), and it was forwarded to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) who had written the minister on behalf of a constituent who was requesting the decentralization of Air Canada's facilities currently located in Montreal. My hon. friend was informed by the Minister of Transport as follows:
Air Canada now has a decentralized organization with much of its staff and facilities located at points across Canada. In this connection, I would point out that an overhaul base will be established in Winnipeg.
So they are building a hangar, and the minister has stated that an overhaul base will be established in Winnipeg. I see no reason for any further delay, and I would suggest that my
[Mr. McKenzie.)
motion be considered immediately and this serious problem presented to the committee which would begin immediate hearings to consider all the complaints and suggestions of the employees, the unions, the Gens de l'Air and any other interested parties in connection with this serious problem, one which I confirmed today when I visited the Dorval Airport.
These are some of the concerns of the Canadian Aviation Fellowship. They want to know what is going to happen to an English-speaking, non-francophone employee whose job is suddenly designated as bilingual or "French-essential". I can understand that question because Bill-101 put forward by a separatist government is designed to drive Anglophones out of Quebec-there is no doubt about that in my mind; it was confirmed today and it is one of the concerns of these employees. There is no way in which we can operate a national airline safely and efficiently under these conditions.
The Aviation Fellowship further asks what is to become of the opportunities for advancement of English-speaking nonFrancophone employees in comparison to those available for Francophone and other bilingual employees. For what jobs would employees be required to take French courses and qualify up to a certain level of competency within a given period? How will this be accomplished?
In a letter to me they point out, further, that the premier of Quebec has already talked about carving up Air Canada after Quebec achieves independence. This, they say, is a very real possibility and cannot be ignored, especially with the Parti Quebecois in power. They add that according to Mr. Levesque's timetable this may well happen within 18 months. The big question is: what is Air Canada's contingency plan to deal with Quebec independence? Never mind acting like ostriches or trying to sweep difficulties under the rug. I have mentioned safety and efficiency. There are other concerns which preoccupy the employees.
Here is an article which appeared in today's Montreal Star. It states:
A committee of priests and laymen speaking for English Catholic parishes in Montreal says that debate on language is producing quarrels in French-English marriages.
In addition to spreading fear among the English and sparking an exodus of both French and English from the province, the committee said in its brief on language that the government's bill is "having a divisive effect" on mixed marriages.

subtopic: INFORMATION-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE CITIZENS WITH RIGHT OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
INFORMATION-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE CITIZENS WITH RIGHT OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some anticipation that I look forward to the opportunity of debating the Prime Minister's answer to my question on February 7, 1977, regarding more freedom of information for Canadians.
The Prime Minister in his answer did not say that we have lesser rights than Americans; he only said that he would not
Adjournment Debate
admit it; and he did not answer my supplementary question as to whether he would consider introducing methods to improve the situation because of the necessity of Canadians having to go to the United States to receive information about their own country. He did not answer that question at all.
But this is still an issue of current interest and importance, Mr. Speaker. For example, it is very significant that a leading Canadian newspaper reported, under yesterday's date, July 11, the speech of Ralph Nader, one of the most important and well respected consumer advocates in the world, broadcast on the CBC, in which he said the following:
In Ottawa secrecy shrouds even the most routine information-auto safety reports, meat and poultry inspections, the specific reasons for government decisions.
He also said that law students working in Washington last year got Canadian government information which was classified secret by using the American law. The law students, after hearing the Canadian government had refused to divulge the information, asked the U.S. postal service for the information and got it. Mr. Nader reminded Canadians that in the United States a government agency can be hauled into court for withholding information from the public. A Canadian information law with similar clout would reduce government corruption and waste, which Mr. Nader argued thrive in secrecy. He said that a Watergate type scandal in Canada would create a stronger push in parliament to pass a freedom of information law.
Never in the history of our country have we had such a secretive and incompetent government. It is a fair comment that the secrecy is partly the result of a desire to hide its incompetence. Nor have we ever had such a misguided or misinformed Prime Minister whose dreary and pedantic pronouncements in parliament have been remarkable only for their consistency in being incorrect. It is not appropriate under the terms of this adjournment debate to provide examples of his previous patently wrong pronouncements about unemployment, inflation, and the death of separatism, thus I will confine myself to examining the inconsistencies in this one about freedom of information.
The Prime Minister must know that in December, 1975, the Joint Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments brought in a report approving the principle of legislation dealing with freedom of information and that the House unanimously accepted and approved this resolution on February 12, 1976.
The Prime Minister must also be aware that at the Liberal policy conference in Toronto last fall, that august body of privileged Canadians not only endorsed the concept of a meaningful freedom of information act, but gave it a standing ovation. In view of the almost unanimous cry for a meaningful freedom of information act coming from the public, the press, interest groups, and all political parties, including the Liberal party, one can only wonder why the government and the Prime
80020-18'/2

July 12, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Minister refuse to enact any freedom of information legislation.
I wonder why the government, in the face of a unanimous resolution of this House and even in the face of the enthusiastic endorsation given to such a proposal by its own party, would continue to refuse to put forward a freedom of information act. The government must have serious reasons if it is prepared to face this almost unanimous demand and to fight to the end for secrecy. In view of the government's part performance, the reason is obvious. This government is the most incompetent, corrupt, and scandal-ridden government in the history of this country. It is determined to see that as little information on its activities as possible is made public because of the likelihood that such information will reveal, as it has so often in the past, that the government's performance has been incompetent and its activities suspicious.
This government is practised and experienced at hiding its activities, shielding them from public scrutiny, and keeping its activities secret, and better than all his ministers of this part of "participatory democracy" is the Prime Minister himself. No one has done more for the cause of secrecy than he.
A partial list only of organizations which agree with the need for meaningful freedom of information legislation is as follows: Canadian Association of University Teachers, Canadian Civil Liberties Association, Canadian Community Newspapers Association, Canadian Labour Congress, Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Consumers Association of Canada, and the last one 1 will mention is the Canadian Bar Association which passed the following resolution on freedom of information:
Whereas openness of government is essential for participatory democracy;
And whereas access to information is a prerequisite to the exercise of other fundamental rights and freedoms;
And whereas the citizens of Canada have no legal right to government information;
Now therefore be it resolved that the Canadian Bar Association urges that access to information legislation be enacted by the Parliament of Canada and all provincial legislatures in Canada creating a statutory right of persons to obtain access to information held by all governments or their agencies, subject only to a limited list of narrowly defined exceptions, with any refusal to provide such information and any unreasonable delay or costs subject to review and enforcement by the courts on the merits with the burden of proof on the government.
It is obvious that this country does not have adequate freedom of information. Mr. Speaker, I rest my case.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mike Landers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INFORMATION-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE CITIZENS WITH RIGHT OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-25 has now been given third reading in both Houses of Parliament. Under part IV of Bill C-25, Canadians will be given a right of access to personal information held on them by government departments and agencies. This is the first time that legislation granting such a right has been enacted in Canada or within a parliamentary system similar to Canada's. The right is not an absolute one, and there is general agreement that it cannot be absolute. The rights of the individual have to be balanced against public interest. Every effort, however, has been made by the government to limit the exemptions to the greatest extent possible. Several amendments to part IV were proposed by the government at committee stage in the House, which served to tighten the exemptions.
The exemptions which have been included in part IV are similar to those contained in the U.S. privacy act. If anything, those in part IV should prove to be somewhat narrower.
No amendments to part IV were moved by members of the opposition in committee or report stages in either the House of Commons or the other place. Although the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) made several adverse comments about part IV, neither he nor anyone in his party actually moved any amendments to it.
In third reading debate in the other place, the Leader of the Opposition in the Senate (Senator Flynn) recognized that the bill opened up a new field of legislation and should be passed into law to see how it operates in practice.
I should point out that if the secret of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) success is being pedantic, perhaps the official opposition should follow suit if they intend to form the government sometime within the next half century.
